- **Convolution Length ($L$):** Determines the spatial extent of the dye.

If this is not pre-computed during the initial LIC pass, computing it on the fly for every neighbor in the BFS can be costly.

The algorithm was proposed in the context of Dye-Advection LIC, an extension of Line Integral Convolution (LIC) that simulates the advection of dye in a vector field.
The standard LIC method convolves a noise texture along streamlines.
Dye advection allows for dynamic visualization of flow features by injecting dye at specific points.

The fast searching algorithm was introduced to solve the problem of efficiently identifying which cells need to be updated when new dye is injected, avoiding the prohibitive memory costs of storing full backward streamline histories [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the fast searching algorithm was introduced to efficiently identify cells needing updates for new dye injection while avoiding the prohibitive memory costs of storing full backward streamline histories. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in Section 3.2. It describes the 'brute force method' of creating lists of all cells stepping backwards (full backward streamline histories) as having 'overwhelming' or 'prohibitive' memory requirements. It then introduces the 'fast searching algorithm' which uses a BFS on 'direct flow-back neighbors' to locate a superset of affected cells, noting that this approach is 'considerably more memory efficient' because it only stores direct neighbors rather than full histories.

The second part of the claim, that higher resolution 'may reduce the average number of direct flow-back neighbors if the flow is smooth', is not supported by the evidence, which only provides a static average (2 or 3) for experimental 3D flows without discussing the effect of resolution changes on this metric.
